chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Sinān, from Ibn Muskān, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about wudu (ablution) from water into which a dog had lapped, or a cat, or from which a camel or a beast or something else had drunk: may wudu (ablution) be performed from it, or ghusl? He said: Yes, unless you find other than it, then avoid it.

So this report is not contrary to the earlier reports, because the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as referring to when the water is kurr or more than that; and what indicates that is what...

key_terms.الْخَبَرُ: the report or hadith being discussed
key_terms.الْكَلْبُ: the dog, mentioned here in relation to water impurity rulings
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual washing before salat
key_terms.فَتَنَزَّهْ: avoid it and keep away from it out of caution
key_terms.كُرًّا: a legally significant measure of water quantity in ritual purity law
key_terms.وَلَغَ: lapped or drank with the tongue, especially used for an animal's drinking
key_terms.يُغْتَسَلُ: ghusl is performed, meaning ritual bathing with the water

ai.seo_question: Can one perform wudu (ablution) or ghusl with water from which a dog or other animals have drunk?
ai.summary: This report discusses the ruling of using water for wudu (ablution) or ghusl after animals such as a dog, cat, camel, or other beasts have drunk from it. The appended scholarly note explains that the report is reconciled with earlier narrations by understanding it to apply to water that is kurr or greater in quantity.
